title: How to run a design critique in a small team
metaTitle: A design critique process in 30 minutes
excerpt: A design critique process asks whether the work does the job. A founder can host it in thirty minutes if preferences wait until that question is answered.
alt: A workshop where one person points at colorful sticky notes while others sit with laptops. The notes are the job the critique should test, not a pile of preferences.
caption: Point at the job, then at the work. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: How long should a design critique take in a small team?
faqs.answer: Thirty minutes is enough when the job is written down and the work can be opened. Spend the first minutes on the goal, most of the time on whether the work meets it, and the last minutes on decisions with owners. A critique that runs until people are tired is collecting preferences, not finishing a review.

faqs.question: Who should speak, and in what order?
faqs.answer: The person who made the work states the job and the constraint, then stops. Everyone else looks before they talk. Comments start with the person who will use the result, if they are in the room, because their hesitation is evidence. The founder speaks to accept or reject a change, not to fill the silence.

faqs.question: What kind of comment is out of bounds?
faqs.answer: A comment that only names a personal taste, with no link to the job, waits until the decisions are written. "I don't like the blue" is not yet a critique. "The action is hard to find because it matches the blue of the labels" is a critique, because it names a failure against the job.

sources.title: How Long Do Users Stay on Web Pages?

markdown:
A design critique process asks whether the work does the job. It is a short meeting with a decision at the end. It is not a tour of what each person prefers. In a small team the founder can host it. Thirty minutes is the right length if the goal is written down and the work can be opened. Longer meetings feel thorough and usually wander into taste.

The point of keeping it short is honesty. A critique that cannot finish in half an hour is usually missing a job statement, or it is reviewing five screens when it should review one. Bring one flow. Save the rest for the next half hour on another day.

## What you put on the table

Open with the job in one sentence, spoken by the person who made the work. Who it is for, what they are trying to finish, and what must not change. Then name the constraint that mattered: time, a technical limit, or a line counsel asked you to keep. People cannot judge work against a goal they have not heard.

Show the work in the form the user will meet. A staging link is better than a slide. A phone in a hand is better than a wide frame when the job happens on a phone. If you only have a Figma file, walk the path the person takes, including the empty screen and the error, not a highlight reel of the polished frames.

Then stop presenting. A critique dies when the maker narrates every choice before anyone has looked. Silence is part of the method. Two minutes of looking will surface more useful comments than ten minutes of explanation. Write the job sentence where everyone can see it, on a note or at the top of the file, so later comments can be pointed back at it.

## A thirty-minute shape

Use a clock. The shape is the whole process.

1. Five minutes. Read the job and the constraint. Confirm you are reviewing this flow, not the entire product.
2. Ten minutes. Walk the path without defending it. One person uses the work. Others write what they notice. No solutions yet.
3. Ten minutes. Comments, each tied to the job. The useful form is "the person cannot tell what to do next" or "this step adds nothing they did not already know."
4. Five minutes. Decide. Each accepted comment becomes a change with an owner. Each rejected comment gets one sentence of reason. Stop when the time stops.

If you finish early, end early. Do not fill the remaining minutes with new ideas. New ideas are a different meeting. This one is a test of the work already on the table. Parking a new idea on the later list is allowed. Designing it live is how the thirty minutes becomes ninety.

Nielsen Norman Group's 2011 article on how long people stay on web pages is a good standard for the ten-minute walk. People often leave within 10 to 20 seconds when a page's value is unclear, and they read only about a quarter of the text. [The research](https://www.nngroup.com/articles/how-long-do-users-stay-on-web-pages/) is about web pages, and it still disciplines a product critique. If the job is not visible at the start of the path, the rest of the screens are a debate about words many people will never reach. Say that in the room. It keeps the group from polishing paragraph three.

## Comments that belong, and comments that wait

A comment belongs when it claims the work fails the job, and when someone can point at the spot. "The price is below the photograph, so I did not see it before the button" is a claim you can check. "Make it pop" is a mood. Ask the speaker to restate a mood as a failure. If they cannot, write it down as a preference and leave it out of the decision list.

Preferences are allowed to exist. They are not allowed to restart the layout during the critique. Collect them in the margin. After the decisions are done, look at the margin only if there is time and the change is cheap. A typeface someone dislikes, which still reads and still matches the brand you agreed, is a preference. A typeface that fails at the size on a phone is a job failure, because the person cannot read the offer.

The maker may answer a comment with a constraint. "We tried that and the name has to stay for legal reasons" is a useful answer. "I already thought about that" is not. The second answer closes the room. The first one updates the job statement so the next comment is smarter.

In a team of a few people, roles blur. The founder is often the maker, the approver, and the user. Split those roles out loud for the half hour. While you are the maker, you do not also get to be the only critic. Ask someone else to walk the path. If everyone in the company already knows the product too well, borrow one person from outside the work for the ten-minute walk. A customer, an advisor, or a new hire in their first week will hesitate in places you no longer see.

## End with a list, not a vibe

The last five minutes produce a short list. Each line is a change, an owner, and what done means. "Clarify the hero" is not a line. "Rewrite the first sentence so it names the buyer and the outcome" is a line. "Look at mobile" is not a line. "Put the primary action under the offer on a narrow screen" is a line.

Rejecting a comment is also a result. Write the reason next to it so the same comment does not return next week as if it were new. A critique without a written ending will be remembered differently by every person who attended. The document is the critique. The conversation is how you got there.

Do not add a second round of design inside the meeting. If a comment requires a new direction, schedule the work. Trying to sketch the replacement while the clock runs produces a half-idea that nobody quite agreed to, which is the hardest kind of feedback to build. Hanabi runs critiques this way on purpose. The studio would rather leave with three owned changes than with a whiteboard full of maybes.

## After the meeting

Send the list the same day, in the channel the team already uses. Include the job sentence so a reader who missed the meeting can still understand the changes. The people who were there should be able to start without a second conversation about what was meant.

The way a client, or a founder, gives notes back to a studio is a related skill. A critique inside the team and a round of feedback on someone else's work fail in the same way when the notes abandon the goal. Read [how to give design feedback without restarting the project](/blog/feedback-that-does-not-restart-the-work) when the next step is responding to work you did not draw yourself.

If you want a studio in the room for that kind of half hour, book [an intro call](https://cal.com/hanabi/30min). The call should decide whether a project fits. It is not itself a free critique of your whole product.
